meta.title: FDE Knowledge Graph: Measurement, Trust, Discovery, Structure & Change
meta.source: Synthesized from general knowledge of the books (no book text ingested). Descriptions are paraphrases, not quotes.

books.htma: How to Measure Anything (Douglas W. Hubbard)
books.ta: The Trusted Advisor (David H. Maister, Charles H. Green, Robert M. Galford)
books.bps: Bulletproof Problem Solving (Charles Conn, Robert McLean)
books.fde: Synthesis layer: Forward Deployed Engineering practice

nodes.label: How to Measure Anything
nodes.description: Argues that anything that matters to a decision can be measured, where measurement means reducing uncertainty, not achieving certainty. Introduces Applied Information Economics (AIE).

nodes.label: The Trusted Advisor
nodes.description: How professional advisors earn and keep client trust. Introduces the Trust Equation and a five-step trust-building process.

nodes.label: The Mom Test
nodes.description: How to talk to customers and learn whether a business is a good idea when everyone is lying to you (politely). Conversations should produce facts about the customer's life, not opinions about your idea.

nodes.label: Douglas W. Hubbard
nodes.description: Management consultant, creator of Applied Information Economics (AIE).

nodes.label: David H. Maister
nodes.description: Authority on professional services firm management.

nodes.label: Charles H. Green
nodes.description: Co-author; later developed the Trust Equation work further (Trusted Advisor Associates).

nodes.label: Robert M. Galford
nodes.description: Co-author; advisor and educator on leadership and trust.

nodes.label: Rob Fitzpatrick
nodes.description: Founder and author; wrote The Mom Test from his own failed customer-discovery experiences.

nodes.label: Measurement = Uncertainty Reduction
nodes.description: A measurement is a quantitatively expressed reduction of uncertainty based on one or more observations. It does not need to eliminate uncertainty to be valuable.

nodes.label: Clarification Chain
nodes.description: If something matters, it is detectable/observable; if it is detectable, it can be detected as an amount (or range); if it can be detected as a range, it can be measured. Used to turn 'intangibles' into observables.

nodes.label: Illusions of Intangibility
nodes.description: Three reasons people believe something can't be measured: misunderstanding the Concept of measurement, the Object of measurement (it's ill-defined), and the Methods of measurement (unaware of sampling, Bayes, etc.).

nodes.label: Four Useful Measurement Assumptions
nodes.description: (1) Your problem is not as unique as you think. (2) You have more data than you think. (3) You need less data than you think. (4) Useful new data is more accessible than you think.

nodes.label: Applied Information Economics (AIE)
nodes.description: Hubbard's method: (1) define the decision, (2) model current uncertainty with calibrated estimates, (3) compute the value of additional information, (4) measure only where information value is high, (5) decide and act.

nodes.label: Define the Decision First
nodes.description: Measurement only has value if it can change a decision. Start by stating the decision, the alternatives, and what 'the thing' you want to measure actually means in observable terms.

nodes.label: Calibrated Estimation
nodes.description: Training people so that their stated confidence matches their actual hit rate (e.g., 90% of their 90% intervals contain the truth). Most untrained experts are overconfident.

nodes.label: 90% Confidence Interval
nodes.description: Express current knowledge as a range you are 90% sure contains the true value, instead of a single point or 'we don't know'.

nodes.label: Equivalent Bet Test
nodes.description: Calibration aid: would you rather bet on your range containing the answer or on a spin with a 90% chance of winning? Adjust the range until you are indifferent.

nodes.label: Overconfidence Bias
nodes.description: Experts systematically give ranges that are too narrow. Calibration training corrects it.

nodes.label: Decomposition (Fermi)
nodes.description: Break an uncertain quantity into components that are easier to estimate. Often decomposition alone reduces uncertainty enough that no further measurement is needed.

nodes.label: Expected Value of Information (EVI)
nodes.description: The expected reduction in opportunity loss from gaining more information. The value of perfect information (EVPI) equals the expected opportunity loss of the current best choice.

nodes.label: Expected Opportunity Loss (EOL)
nodes.description: Chance of being wrong times the cost of being wrong. Information is valuable to the extent it reduces EOL.

nodes.label: Measurement Inversion
nodes.description: Organizations tend to measure what is easy and low-value and ignore the high-uncertainty, high-value variables that would actually change decisions.

nodes.label: Monte Carlo Simulation
nodes.description: Propagate calibrated ranges through a model to get a distribution of outcomes (e.g., ROI, risk of loss) instead of a single point estimate.

nodes.label: Rule of Five
nodes.description: With a random sample of 5, there is a 93.75% chance the population median lies between the smallest and largest value. Small samples reduce uncertainty a lot when you know little.

nodes.label: Single Sample Majority Rule
nodes.description: ('Urn of Mystery') With total uncertainty about a proportion, one random sample gives a 75% chance of identifying the majority. The first observations are the most informative.

nodes.label: Bayesian Updating
nodes.description: Start from calibrated priors and update with each new observation, rather than demanding large samples before saying anything.

nodes.label: Stated vs. Revealed Preferences
nodes.description: Measure values and preferences by what people actually do or pay (revealed) rather than only by what they say (stated). Includes willingness-to-pay methods.

nodes.label: Critique of Scoring / Risk Matrices
nodes.description: Ordinal scores (high/medium/low, 1-5) add ambiguity and can make decisions worse than unaided intuition. Prefer probabilistic, quantitative models.

nodes.label: You Need Less Data Than You Think
nodes.description: When uncertainty is high, a little data goes a long way. Marginal value of each extra observation drops quickly.

nodes.label: Trust Equation
nodes.description: Trustworthiness = (Credibility + Reliability + Intimacy) / Self-Orientation.

nodes.label: Credibility
nodes.description: Words: expertise, accuracy, honesty about what you know and don't know. 'I can trust what they say.'

nodes.label: Reliability
nodes.description: Actions: repeated experience of doing what you said, when you said. 'I can trust them to do it.'

nodes.label: Intimacy
nodes.description: Emotions: safety the client feels in sharing difficult or sensitive things. 'I can talk to them about this.'

nodes.label: Self-Orientation
nodes.description: The denominator: focus on yourself (appearing smart, winning the sale, being right) rather than on the client. The largest lever on trust.

nodes.label: Five-Step Trust Process
nodes.description: Engage → Listen → Frame → Envision → Commit. The sequence through which trust is built in an advisory interaction.

nodes.label: Engage
nodes.description: Get the client's attention on an issue that matters to them, showing you've done your homework on their world.

nodes.label: Listen
nodes.description: Understand both the rational content and the emotional reality. Listening earns the right to offer a perspective.

nodes.label: Frame
nodes.description: Articulate the real problem, often reframing the presenting issue. Includes 'naming and claiming' difficult topics.

nodes.label: Envision
nodes.description: Jointly describe an alternative future: what would be different, concretely, if the problem were solved.

nodes.label: Commit
nodes.description: Agree on concrete next steps and mutual obligations; the client takes ownership of the path forward.

nodes.label: Earning the Right
nodes.description: Advisors must earn the right to give advice, typically through demonstrated listening and understanding, before offering solutions.

nodes.label: Name It and Claim It
nodes.description: Openly naming the awkward, risky, or emotional issue ('this may be uncomfortable, but...') and taking responsibility for raising it.

nodes.label: Advisor Evolution
nodes.description: Progression from subject-matter/service provider → needs-based problem solver → relationship-based → trust-based advisor consulted on broad, strategic issues.

nodes.label: Client Owns the Decision
nodes.description: Good advice gives options and reasoning; the client makes the choice. Imposing answers erodes trust.

nodes.label: Relationship over Transaction
nodes.description: Trust is built over repeated interactions; optimize for the long-term relationship, not the current deal.

nodes.label: Emotional Reality of Clients
nodes.description: Clients often feel insecure, exposed, or anxious when they need help. Recognizing these emotions is part of professional skill.

nodes.label: Need to Be Right / Appear Smart
nodes.description: A common driver of high self-orientation: jumping to answers, showing off expertise, or arguing instead of understanding.

nodes.label: The Mom Test Rules
nodes.description: (1) Talk about their life instead of your idea. (2) Ask about specifics in the past instead of generics or opinions about the future. (3) Talk less and listen more.

nodes.label: Talk About Their Life, Not Your Idea
nodes.description: Once you mention your idea, people start being nice to you. Ask about their problems, workflows, and goals instead.

nodes.label: Past Specifics over Future Generics
nodes.description: 'Talk me through the last time that happened' beats 'Would you ever...?'. Past behavior is data; predictions about the future are optimistic fiction.

nodes.label: Talk Less, Listen More
nodes.description: The more you talk, the less you learn. Avoid pitching during discovery.

nodes.label: Bad Data
nodes.description: Three types of misleading signal: compliments, fluff (generic claims, hypotheticals, future promises), and ideas (feature requests).

nodes.label: Compliments
nodes.description: 'That sounds great!' is worthless data and a sign you're pitching. Deflect them and return to facts.

nodes.label: Fluff
nodes.description: Generic ('I usually...'), future-tense ('I would...'), and hypothetical statements. Anchor them to specific past examples.

nodes.label: Ideas & Feature Requests
nodes.description: Requests should not be taken at face value. Dig into the motivation: why do you want that? What would it let you do?

nodes.label: Dig Beneath Requests & Emotions
nodes.description: Ask 'Why do you bother?', 'What are the implications of that?', 'What else have you tried?' to uncover the real problem and its severity.

nodes.label: Commitment & Advancement
nodes.description: A meeting succeeds only if it ends with commitment (they give up something of value) and advancement (move to the next step in the buying/learning process).

nodes.label: Currencies of Commitment
nodes.description: Time (follow-up meetings, trials), reputation risk (intros to boss/peers), and money (pre-orders, deposits, LOIs).

nodes.label: Zombie Leads / False Positives
nodes.description: Meetings that 'went well' with no commitment. Lukewarm interest that never converts; better to get a clear no.

nodes.label: Ask the Scary Questions
nodes.description: The important questions are the ones that could kill your idea. Founders avoid them; you should seek them out.

nodes.label: Prepare Your Big 3 Questions
nodes.description: Before each conversation, decide the three most important things you want to learn.

nodes.label: Keep It Casual
nodes.description: Strip away the formality of 'meetings'; casual conversations produce more honest information and are cheaper to run.

nodes.label: Look Before You Zoom
nodes.description: Confirm a problem is a real priority for them before diving into its details; avoid fixating on a 'problem' they don't actually care about.

nodes.label: Customer Slicing (Who-Where)
nodes.description: Keep slicing a broad segment into a specific who you can find (where). Too broad a segment produces contradictory, mushy data.

nodes.label: Vision-Framing-Weakness-Pedestal-Ask
nodes.description: Structure for requesting a learning meeting: share the vision, frame the stage you're in, show weakness (you need help), put them on a pedestal (they can help), and ask.

nodes.label: Take Good Notes & Share Learnings
nodes.description: Record exact quotes and signals (pain, goals, obstacles, workarounds, money) and review them with the team so learning isn't trapped in one head.

nodes.label: Pitching During Discovery
nodes.description: Slipping into pitch mode turns a learning conversation into a sales one and triggers polite lies.

nodes.label: Existing Workarounds & Spend
nodes.description: What they already do, use, or pay to solve the problem is the strongest evidence of a real problem.

nodes.label: Behavior over Opinion
nodes.description: All three books converge: trust evidence of what people did/paid/committed (revealed) over what they say they think or will do (stated).

nodes.label: Customer Conversation as Measurement
nodes.description: A Mom Test interview is a measurement instrument in Hubbard's sense: each observation reduces uncertainty about a decision-relevant variable (pain, frequency, willingness to pay).

nodes.label: Scary Questions Have the Highest Information Value
nodes.description: The questions people avoid (Mom Test) are exactly the high-uncertainty, high-EOL variables that Measurement Inversion warns we neglect. Naming them (Trusted Advisor) builds trust rather than destroying it.

nodes.label: Self-Orientation Corrupts Data
nodes.description: Pitching, needing to be right, and seeking compliments both lower trust (TA denominator) and bias the evidence you gather (Mom Test bad data).

nodes.label: Framing = Defining the Decision
nodes.description: TA's Frame step and HTMA's 'define the decision' are the same move: make explicit what problem is being solved and what choice depends on it.

nodes.label: Envision in Observable Terms
nodes.description: Use the Clarification Chain during TA's Envision step: 'If this were solved, what would you see that you don't see now?' yields measurable success criteria.

nodes.label: Honest Uncertainty Builds Credibility
nodes.description: Giving calibrated ranges instead of false precision or evasive 'it depends' raises Credibility; overconfidence destroys it when reality diverges.

nodes.label: Commitment Is the Real Signal
nodes.description: Mom Test commitment currencies, TA's Commit step, and HTMA's revealed preferences all treat a costly action as the trustworthy measurement of value.

nodes.label: Small Samples Are Enough to Start
nodes.description: Rule of Five and Single Sample Majority justify acting on a handful of well-run interviews when uncertainty is high; keep going until you stop hearing new things.

nodes.label: Discovery Interview
nodes.description: First on-site conversations with users/operators: Big 3 questions, past-specific questions, listen for emotional reality, note workarounds, end with a commitment.

nodes.label: Problem Framing Doc
nodes.description: One page: the decision at stake, alternatives, key uncertain variables (with 90% CIs), and what would change the decision.

nodes.label: Quantified Value Case
nodes.description: Decompose the business value, attach calibrated ranges sourced from interviews and data, run Monte Carlo, and present a distribution rather than a single ROI number.

nodes.label: Pilot Success Criteria
nodes.description: Observable, measurable criteria agreed with the client up front (Envision + Clarification Chain), plus explicit commitments if criteria are met.

nodes.label: What to Measure Next
nodes.description: Prioritize data collection and instrumentation by information value, not by ease. Fight Measurement Inversion in the deployment backlog.

nodes.label: Stakeholder Trust Map
nodes.description: For each stakeholder, assess C/R/I/S, track promises made and kept, and plan which difficult topics need to be named.

nodes.label: Evidence-Based Go/No-Go
nodes.description: Decide expansion or exit based on commitment signals and reduced uncertainty in key variables, not on how well meetings 'felt'.

nodes.label: The Pyramid Principle
nodes.description: How to structure thinking and writing so that busy executives get the answer first, supported by a logically grouped hierarchy of ideas.

nodes.label: Barbara Minto
nodes.description: Former McKinsey consultant who developed the Pyramid Principle for business writing and presentation.

nodes.label: Pyramid Structure
nodes.description: A single governing thought at the top, supported by key-line ideas, each supported by further ideas. Ideas at any level summarize the ideas grouped below them.

nodes.label: Answer First (Top-Down)
nodes.description: Present the conclusion/recommendation first, then the supporting arguments. Readers process ideas more easily when they know where they are going.

nodes.label: Governing Thought
nodes.description: The single top-level message — the answer to the reader's question.

nodes.label: Situation-Complication-Question (SCQ)
nodes.description: Introduction structure: a familiar Situation, a Complication that changes it, the Question that arises — answered by the governing thought.

nodes.label: Vertical Q&A Dialogue
nodes.description: Each statement raises a question in the reader's mind (why? how?) which the level below answers.

nodes.label: Grouping Rules
nodes.description: Ideas in each grouping must be the same kind of idea and logically ordered (time, structure, or degree of importance).

nodes.label: MECE
nodes.description: Mutually Exclusive, Collectively Exhaustive: groupings with no overlaps and no gaps.

nodes.label: Deductive vs. Inductive Logic
nodes.description: Horizontal relationships between ideas: deductive chains (premise → premise → therefore) or inductive groupings (similar ideas pointing to one inference). Minto favors inductive groupings at the key line.

nodes.label: Key Line
nodes.description: The level of ideas directly below the governing thought; the main supporting arguments.

nodes.label: Think Bottom-Up, Present Top-Down
nodes.description: Build the pyramid by grouping detailed findings into summaries, then communicate from the top.

nodes.label: Chronological Analysis Dump
nodes.description: Presenting work in the order it was done ('first we looked at...') instead of leading with the answer; buries the message.

nodes.label: Bulletproof Problem Solving
nodes.description: A seven-step, hypothesis-driven problem-solving method rooted in McKinsey practice, built around logic trees and disciplined prioritization.

nodes.label: Charles Conn
nodes.description: Co-author; former McKinsey partner and CEO of the Rhodes Trust.

nodes.label: Robert McLean
nodes.description: Co-author; former McKinsey director.

nodes.label: Seven-Step Problem Solving
nodes.description: (1) Define the problem, (2) Disaggregate it, (3) Prioritize, (4) Build a workplan, (5) Conduct analyses, (6) Synthesize findings, (7) Communicate. An iterative loop, not a waterfall.

nodes.label: Problem Definition Worksheet
nodes.description: A precise problem statement: specific, measurable, action-oriented; decision-maker, success criteria, scope, constraints, timeframe.

nodes.label: Logic / Issue Trees
nodes.description: Disaggregate a problem into components. Types: component (factor) trees, hypothesis trees, and decision trees.

nodes.label: Hypothesis Tree
nodes.description: Tree that states a hypothesized answer and the conditions that must be true for it to hold; each branch becomes a test.

nodes.label: Hypothesis-Driven Approach
nodes.description: Start with a best-guess answer early and work to prove or disprove it, instead of boiling the ocean.

nodes.label: Prioritization 2x2 (Impact × Influence)
nodes.description: Prune tree branches by size of impact and ability to influence; focus analysis on the critical few.

nodes.label: Workplan & Analysis Plan
nodes.description: For each prioritized branch: hypothesis, analysis needed, data sources, owner, deadline, expected end product.

nodes.label: One-Day Answer
nodes.description: Write the best answer you could give today; refine it as analysis comes in. Keeps work focused on the synthesis.

nodes.label: Heuristics Before Big Guns
nodes.description: Use rules of thumb, order-of-magnitude and back-of-envelope analysis before sophisticated tools (regression, simulation, game theory).

nodes.label: Team Processes Against Bias
nodes.description: Red teams, obligation to dissent, perspective-taking and diverse teams counter confirmation bias and anchoring.

nodes.label: Synthesize & Tell the Story
nodes.description: Turn analyses into a 'so what' storyline, commonly structured as a pyramid, ending in a recommendation.

nodes.label: Confirmation Bias
nodes.description: Hypothesis-driven work's main risk: seeking only evidence that confirms the initial answer.

nodes.label: Wicked Problems
nodes.description: Problems with many interdependent causes and stakeholders and no clear stopping rule; require iteration and systems thinking.

nodes.label: Switch
nodes.description: Why change is hard and how to make it happen: direct the rational side, motivate the emotional side, and shape the environment.

nodes.label: Chip Heath
nodes.description: Stanford professor; co-author with his brother Dan.

nodes.label: Dan Heath
nodes.description: Senior fellow at Duke's CASE center; co-author with his brother Chip.

nodes.label: Rider, Elephant, Path
nodes.description: The Rider is the rational planner, the Elephant is emotion and habit, the Path is the situation. Change requires directing the Rider, motivating the Elephant, and shaping the Path.

nodes.label: Direct the Rider
nodes.description: Give the rational side clarity: find the bright spots, script the critical moves, point to the destination.

nodes.label: Motivate the Elephant
nodes.description: Engage emotion: find the feeling, shrink the change, grow your people.

nodes.label: Shape the Path
nodes.description: Change the situation: tweak the environment, build habits, rally the herd.

nodes.label: Find the Bright Spots
nodes.description: Look for what is already working somewhere and clone it, instead of obsessing over what's broken.

nodes.label: Script the Critical Moves
nodes.description: Translate goals into specific behaviors. Ambiguity exhausts the Rider.

nodes.label: Point to the Destination
nodes.description: A vivid 'destination postcard' and black-and-white goals show where you're going and why it's worth it.

nodes.label: Find the Feeling
nodes.description: People change through see-feel-change more often than analyze-think-change.

nodes.label: Shrink the Change
nodes.description: Make the first step small enough that the Elephant isn't spooked; create early wins.

nodes.label: Grow Your People
nodes.description: Cultivate an identity and growth mindset that make the change feel like 'who we are'.

nodes.label: Tweak the Environment
nodes.description: Small changes to the situation (defaults, friction, layout, tooling) can produce big behavior changes.

nodes.label: Build Habits
nodes.description: Action triggers and checklists make new behavior automatic and cheap for the Rider.

nodes.label: Rally the Herd
nodes.description: Behavior is contagious; make the desired behavior visible and socially normal.

nodes.label: Resistance Is Often Lack of Clarity
nodes.description: What looks like resistance is often lack of clarity; what looks like laziness is often exhaustion; what looks like a people problem is often a situation problem.

nodes.label: Decision Paralysis
nodes.description: Too many options or ambiguity freeze the Rider and default people to the status quo.

nodes.label: Flawless Consulting
nodes.description: A guide to consulting without direct authority: contracting, discovery, feedback, and above all dealing authentically with client resistance.

nodes.label: Peter Block
nodes.description: Organizational development consultant and author on consulting, stewardship and community.

nodes.label: Five Phases of Consulting
nodes.description: Entry & Contracting → Discovery & Dialogue → Feedback & Decision to Act → Engagement & Implementation → Extension, Recycle or Termination.

nodes.label: Contracting
nodes.description: Explicit agreement on wants and offers from both client and consultant: what each needs, expects, and will provide, including the client's own involvement.

nodes.label: Discovery & Dialogue
nodes.description: Collecting data and building a shared picture of the problem, including how the problem is being managed, not just the technical problem.

nodes.label: Feedback Meeting
nodes.description: Present findings simply and descriptively, then focus on the client's reactions and the decision to act; expect resistance here.

nodes.label: Consultant Roles
nodes.description: Expert (consultant decides), Pair-of-Hands (client decides, consultant executes), Collaborative (joint diagnosis and shared responsibility). Block advocates collaboration.

nodes.label: 50/50 Responsibility
nodes.description: Responsibility for the project's success is shared; the consultant should not take on 100%.

nodes.label: Client Resistance
nodes.description: An emotional reaction to loss of control and vulnerability, not a rational objection. It is predictable and a sign that something important is being touched.

nodes.label: Forms of Resistance
nodes.description: e.g., demanding more detail, flooding you with detail, 'no time', impracticality, attack, confusion, silence, intellectualizing, moralizing, premature compliance, methodology debates.

nodes.label: Name the Resistance
nodes.description: (1) Identify the form it is taking, (2) name it in neutral, non-punishing language, (3) be quiet and let the client respond. Don't take it personally or fight it with more data.

nodes.label: Authenticity
nodes.description: Put into words what you are experiencing with the client as you work. Authentic behavior is the most powerful consulting tool.

nodes.label: Technical vs. Relationship Dimension
nodes.description: Every engagement has a business/technical problem and a relationship/how-it's-managed dimension; both must be attended to.

nodes.label: Fighting Resistance with Logic
nodes.description: Answering emotional resistance with more data and argument intensifies it.

nodes.label: Continuous Discovery Habits
nodes.description: A structured, sustainable way for product teams to discover what to build: weekly customer touchpoints in pursuit of a desired outcome.

nodes.label: Teresa Torres
nodes.description: Product discovery coach (Product Talk).

nodes.label: Continuous Discovery
nodes.description: At a minimum, weekly touchpoints with customers by the team building the product, where they conduct small research activities in pursuit of a desired outcome.

nodes.label: Product Trio
nodes.description: Product manager, designer and engineer jointly owning discovery decisions.

nodes.label: Outcomes over Outputs
nodes.description: Teams should be managed by measurable outcomes (business and product outcomes) rather than a roadmap of features (outputs).

nodes.label: Opportunity Solution Tree
nodes.description: Desired outcome → opportunities (customer needs, pain points, desires) → solutions → assumption tests. Makes the team's thinking visible.

nodes.label: Opportunity Space
nodes.description: Customer needs, pain points and desires discovered through interviews, structured as a tree; prioritize opportunities before solutions.

nodes.label: Story-Based Interviewing
nodes.description: Ask for specific stories about past behavior ('Tell me about the last time you...') to learn what actually happens.

nodes.label: Interview Snapshots
nodes.description: One-page synthesis of each interview: memorable quote, quick facts, insights, opportunities, experience map.

nodes.label: Automate Interview Recruiting
nodes.description: Make weekly interviews effortless by building a continuous recruiting pipeline (in-product prompts, support, sales).

nodes.label: Experience Mapping
nodes.description: Map the customer's current experience to frame the opportunity space and align the trio.

nodes.label: Compare and Contrast Decisions
nodes.description: Consider multiple solutions for the same opportunity rather than 'whether or not' decisions about a single idea.

nodes.label: Assumption Mapping
nodes.description: Identify assumptions (desirability, viability, feasibility, usability, ethical) and plot by importance vs. evidence to find leap-of-faith assumptions.

nodes.label: Assumption Testing
nodes.description: Test the riskiest assumptions with small, fast experiments rather than testing whole ideas.

nodes.label: Whether-or-Not Decisions / Solution Fixation
nodes.description: Falling in love with a single solution and evaluating only whether to build it.

nodes.label: Show Your Work to Stakeholders
nodes.description: Share the OST and discovery artifacts so stakeholders see the reasoning, not just conclusions.

nodes.label: Structured Decomposition (Trees Everywhere)
nodes.description: Issue trees, OSTs, the Pyramid and Fermi decomposition are the same move: break a fuzzy whole into MECE, testable parts.

nodes.label: Start with a Hypothesis, Then Measure
nodes.description: Answer-first (Minto), hypothesis-driven work and the one-day answer (Conn & McLean), and calibrated priors updated by data (Hubbard) all start with a best guess and iterate.

nodes.label: Test the Riskiest Assumption First
nodes.description: Assumption mapping (Torres), EVI (Hubbard), the impact × influence 2x2 (Conn & McLean) and scary questions (Fitzpatrick) prioritize what could most change the decision.

nodes.label: Resistance Is Information, Not Opposition
nodes.description: Block's emotional resistance, Switch's 'resistance is lack of clarity', and the Trusted Advisor's emotional reality all say: diagnose and name it; don't argue it away.

nodes.label: Contract Commitments Explicitly
nodes.description: Block's contracting, the Trusted Advisor's Commit step and the Mom Test's commitment currencies: make mutual obligations and next steps explicit.

nodes.label: Outcomes over Outputs
nodes.description: Torres's outcomes, Switch's destination, a precise problem definition and fighting measurement inversion all anchor work on observable change, not activity.

nodes.label: Small Bets Reduce Risk and Resistance
nodes.description: Shrinking the change (Heath), small assumption tests (Torres) and small samples (Hubbard) lower both uncertainty and emotional resistance.

nodes.label: Answer-First Recommendations with Honest Ranges
nodes.description: Lead with the recommendation (Minto) but carry calibrated uncertainty (Hubbard) so credibility survives when reality diverges (Trusted Advisor).

nodes.label: Fix the Situation, Not the People
nodes.description: Adoption failures in deployments are usually path problems (workflow, defaults, tooling) — the same evidence Mom Test workarounds and bright spots reveal.

nodes.label: Engagement Contracting
nodes.description: Kickoff where wants/offers, success criteria, client involvement and decision rights are made explicit (Block), framed as a problem definition (Conn & McLean).

nodes.label: Issue Tree & Workplan
nodes.description: Hypothesis tree for the deployment problem, pruned by impact × influence and information value, with a workplan per branch.

nodes.label: Executive Recommendation Memo
nodes.description: SCQ intro, answer first, MECE key line, quantified value with ranges, explicit ask.

nodes.label: Adoption / Change Plan
nodes.description: Rider-Elephant-Path plan for end users: bright-spot users, scripted critical moves, a small first step, and workflow/tooling tweaks.

nodes.label: Resistance Playbook
nodes.description: Recognize the form of resistance in feedback meetings, name it neutrally, pause; diagnose clarity vs. emotion vs. situation.

nodes.label: Deployment Opportunity Solution Tree
nodes.description: Run the deployment like a product: target outcome, opportunities from weekly user touchpoints, multiple solutions, assumption tests.

nodes.label: Porpoising (Zoom-in / Zoom-out)
nodes.description: Iteratively switching between the high-level strategic system view (macro) and granular operational data (micro) during problem definition.

nodes.label: Red Team & Obligation to Dissent
nodes.description: Institutionalizing contrary perspectives to stress-test the governing hypothesis before presenting findings to executives.

nodes.label: Five Assumption Types (D-V-F-U-E)
nodes.description: Categorizing risks into Desirability, Viability, Feasibility, Usability, and Ethical assumptions prior to running experiments.

nodes.label: Leading Product Outcomes
nodes.description: Short-term observable user behaviors that act as leading indicators for lagging enterprise financial metrics.

nodes.label: Instant Passive Compliance
nodes.description: A subtle form of client resistance where immediate agreement masks an unwillingness to execute or allocate resources.

nodes.label: Neutral Naming Protocol
nodes.description: The exact 3-step sequence: (1) Identify the resistance form, (2) name it without judgment, (3) remain completely silent.

nodes.label: Expected Value of Sample Information (EVSI)
nodes.description: The expected value of imperfect or noisy sample data. Always bounded above by EVPI and used to cap real-world experimentation costs.

nodes.label: Brunswik Lens Model for Expert Judgment
nodes.description: Deconstructing expert decisions into statistical cues to remove human inconsistency, cognitive fatigue, and noise.

nodes.label: Calibrated Estimation Workshop
nodes.description: A pre-modeling workshop where operational leaders and engineers undergo the Equivalent Bet drill to calibrate 90% CIs on baseline failure rates.

nodes.label: Deflecting Compliments
nodes.description: Tactical pivot away from positive praise back to historical facts, budgets, and current operational workarounds.

nodes.label: Advancement Test
nodes.description: Checking whether a customer meeting advances to a clear next commitment or terminates in pleasant, non-committal chatter.

nodes.label: Action Titles (Slide Discipline)
nodes.description: Formulating every slide title as a complete, assertive takeaway sentence rather than a passive topic label.

nodes.label: Three Logical Orders (Time, Structure, Degree)
nodes.description: Rules for organizing horizontal thoughts: chronological sequence (time), structural partition (space/organization), or ranked importance (degree).

nodes.label: Action Triggers (Implementation Intentions)
nodes.description: Pre-deciding the specific time and location to execute a behavior ('When X happens, I do Y') to bypass Rider cognitive exhaustion.

nodes.label: Endowed Progress Effect
nodes.description: People are far more motivated to complete a goal when they feel they have already made progress rather than starting from zero.

nodes.label: Trust Quotient (TQ) Assessment
nodes.description: A 20-question psychometric instrument measuring individual scores across Credibility, Reliability, Intimacy, and Self-Orientation.

nodes.label: Trust Temperaments
nodes.description: Behavioral profiles (Expert, Steward, Connector, Catalyst) that describe how consultants default to building trust with clients.
